idiom_name: Fiber scheduler (Fiber.set_scheduler) with an event-loop gem such as Async
implementation_notes: Ruby core ships the hook rather than the loop: Fiber.set_scheduler registers an object implementing Fiber::SchedulerInterface (io_wait, io_read, io_write, kernel_sleep, block, unblock), and while one is installed, blocking operations park the fiber instead of the thread so the scheduler can resume it when the operation completes. An event-loop library - the Async gem is the dominant one - implements that interface, so the library, not the language, is the completion dispatcher and its task tree is the handler structure. Without a scheduler the honest fallback is threads plus Queue, which is the pattern's threaded engine.
code_sketch:
require "async"

Async do |task|
  server = TCPServer.new(8080)
  loop do
    socket = server.accept          # fiber parks until completion
    task.async { socket.write("ok"); socket.close }
  end
end
pitfalls: Only operations routed through the scheduler are non-blocking; a C extension or a call that ignores the scheduler freezes the whole reactor.
Fibers must be resumed by the scheduler rather than across arbitrary threads, and thread-local state shared between fibers of one thread is a common source of confusion.
Unbounded task creation replaces bounded worker pools and hides back-pressure; Async task trees must be bounded explicitly.
Timeouts and cancellation are manual: a task that waits forever keeps its fiber and any buffers it holds alive.
